source.title: In Favor of the Sensitive Man, and Other Essays
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of In Favor of the Sensitive Man, and Other Essays by Anaïs Nin (1976). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author's estate or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright. Ideas from The Novel of the Future (1968) are kept in the separate source novel-of-the-future-nin, not here.

cards.title: When gatekeepers say no, find another way to publish
cards.body:
In 'The Story of My Printing Press', Nin recalls how American publishers turned down her books in the 1940s as uncommercial. Instead of accepting their verdict, she bought a second-hand, foot-powered press, borrowed small sums from friends, learned to set type from library books, and printed the books herself.

A good review followed and commercial publishers took notice. Her story is an early case for what many creators do today: if the official doors stay closed, build a small door of your own and reach readers directly.
cards.apply_it: Identify one project waiting on someone else's approval. What is one way you could share a small version of it yourself?

quiz.question: What did Nin do when publishers rejected her books?
options: Bought a small printing press and printed them herself
quiz.explanation: She printed and distributed her own books on a second-hand press.

cards.title: Slow, hands-on work shows you what's unnecessary
cards.body:
Setting every letter of a page by hand, Nin writes in the same essay, changed how she wrote. After living with one page for a whole day, she could see which words were not needed. The labour taught her economy.

Most of us now write and delete instantly, so words come cheap. Her experience suggests a useful trick: slow down with your most important work, read it as if each word cost effort, and cut what doesn't earn its place.
cards.apply_it: Take a message or document you wrote today and remove every word that isn't doing a job.

quiz.question: What did hand-setting type teach Nin about writing?
options: To spot and cut unnecessary words
quiz.explanation: Spending a day on one page showed her which words were not needed.

cards.title: Opposition can hand you independence
cards.body:
Looking back on her printing years, Nin admits the work was exhausting and took time from her writing. Yet she says she was glad of the opposition she met, because it gave her independence, confidence and a direct link with readers that sustained her for years. She also concluded that publishers' choices did not truly reflect what the public wanted.

Rejection feels like a wall at the time. Her story shows it can also push you to build skills and relationships no gatekeeper can take away.
cards.apply_it: Recall a past rejection. Write one skill or connection you gained because of it.

quiz.question: How did Nin come to view the opposition she faced from publishers?
options: As the end of her career
As proof her work was poor
As something that gave her independence and confidence
quiz.explanation: She was glad of it in the end because it gave her independence and direct contact with readers.

cards.title: Make room for your own growth without guilt
cards.body:
In 'The New Woman', Nin pictures a woman who feels no guilt about creating or about developing herself. She is calm and confident, and she can ask for space of her own without apologising.

Nin was writing about women in the 1970s, but the trap she describes is common to many people: feeling that time spent on your own learning or art is selfish. She argues the opposite. Growing as a person is not stolen from others; it is part of what you have to give them.
cards.apply_it: Block out one hour this week for something that develops you, and protect it without apologising.

quiz.question: What quality does Nin give the 'new woman'?
options: She feels free of guilt about creating and growing
quiz.explanation: Nin describes her as free of guilt for creating and for her own development.

cards.title: Carry your inner world with you like a diver's air supply
cards.body:
In 'On Truth and Reality', Nin argues that a person's private inner world, built from what they love, imagine and value, is a source of strength and energy, not an escape. She compares it to the oxygen a deep-sea diver carries: you take it with you so you can survive the pressure outside.

Work, news and other people's demands can crush us if we have nothing of our own to draw on. Tending your inner life is how you stay able to face the outer one.
cards.apply_it: Write down three things that feed your inner world. Make time for one of them today.

quiz.question: What does Nin compare a person's inner world to?
options: The oxygen a deep-sea diver carries
quiz.explanation: She uses the image of a diver's oxygen: something you carry to withstand outside pressure.

cards.title: Say what you want, not only what you resent
cards.body:
In the collection's essays on women and men, Nin urges women to stop simply listing grievances against men and to work out, and state, what they actually want. She calls for each person to examine herself honestly rather than follow a ready-made model of womanhood.

The advice applies to anyone in a conflict. Complaints describe what is wrong; clear wishes give the other person something to act on. And you can only state your wishes once you have taken the time to know them.
cards.apply_it: Turn one recent complaint into a clear request that begins with 'What I would like is…'.

quiz.question: What did Nin urge women to do instead of only listing grievances?
options: Examine themselves and say what they want
quiz.explanation: She called for self-examination and clearly stating desires rather than just complaints.

cards.title: Strength and sensitivity belong to everyone
cards.body:
In the title essay and others in the book, Nin welcomes men who are open about feeling, and relationships built as partnerships rather than around one person's career. Drawing on Jung, she suggests that men and women can each develop qualities usually assigned to the other sex.

The point is not to swap roles but to widen them. A man who can show tenderness and a woman who can show ambition are both more whole, and their relationships are more equal.
cards.apply_it: Name one quality you were taught 'isn't for people like you'. Practise it in a small way this week.

quiz.question: What does Nin suggest about qualities traditionally assigned to one sex?
options: Both men and women can develop them
quiz.explanation: Drawing on Jung, she argued both sexes can embrace traits usually given to the other.

cards.title: Asserting yourself doesn't have to mean cutting ties
cards.body:
In the title essay, Nin notes that many women experience any separation as a loss, as if an old bond still governed their emotional lives. So every act of independence can feel like a threat to family and love.

Naming this feeling is the first step to loosening it. Choosing your own path, voicing a different opinion or taking a job far away can be done while keeping relationships warm. Growth and closeness are not opposites, even when it feels that way.
cards.apply_it: Think of a step toward independence you've delayed. Write one way to take it while staying close to the people involved.

quiz.question: According to Nin's title essay, why can self-assertion feel threatening to many women?
options: Separation can feel like a loss of ties
quiz.explanation: She observed that separation carries a feeling of loss, so assertion seems to threaten bonds.
